metadata.title: Action potential: Na+ influx depolarizes, K+ efflux repolarizes
metadata.subject: Biology
metadata.objective: Connect ion permeability changes to depolarization and repolarization.
misconceptions: Na+ leaves the cell during depolarization
metadata.expectedUnderstanding: Resting potential is about -70 mV inside relative to outside. A stimulus depolarizes the membrane to threshold, about -55 mV. At threshold voltage-gated Na+ channels open and Na+ enters, so the inside becomes positive (peak about +30 mV): depolarization is Na+ influx. Na+ channels then inactivate while voltage-gated K+ channels open and K+ leaves, driving the potential back down: repolarization is an active K+ efflux, not passive decay. Slow K+ channel closure overshoots below rest (the undershoot), and the membrane then returns to rest.

primitives.text: Action potential: Na+ influx depolarizes, K+ efflux repolarizes

checkpoints.prompt: The membrane is at rest and the trace is about to leave the baseline. Which ion must cross the membrane first, and in which direction, to start a depolarization?
The probe is parked at the threshold line while the upstroke begins. Are voltage-gated Na+ channels opening or closing there?
During the downstroke, is Na+ entering the cell or leaving it?
The trace is below rest. Which ion's permeability is still above its resting value, and what would happen if it stayed there?

narration.text: At rest the inside of the cell is about -70 mV relative to the outside, and most Na+ channels are closed.
A stimulus depolarizes the membrane: the potential moves up toward the dashed threshold line at about -55 mV.
At threshold, voltage-gated Na+ channels open. Na+ enters the cell and positive charge flows in, so the potential climbs steeply to about +30 mV.
Depolarization is Na+ influx, not efflux: the ions move in the direction their electrochemical gradient pushes them.
Na+ channels inactivate, and voltage-gated K+ channels open. K+ leaves the cell, carrying positive charge out and pulling the potential back down.
K+ channels close slowly, so efflux continues past the resting level: the trace dips below rest, and that undershoot is also active K+ efflux, not a passive decay.
With permeability back near resting values the potential settles at about -70 mV, while the ion gradients themselves are restored by the pumps.

fallback.text: A single static voltage-versus-time trace. Horizontal axis is time; the resting level is about -70 mV, a dashed horizontal line marks threshold at about -55 mV, and the peak is about +30 mV. The trace runs: flat at -70, a short rise to the threshold line, a steep upstroke to +30 labelled Na+ influx, a steep fall through rest to about -80 labelled K+ efflux, then a return to -70. A table beside it lists the phases in order with the ion that drives each one: resting (K+ leak), threshold (Na+ channels opening), upstroke (Na+ in), downstroke (K+ out), undershoot (slow K+ channel closure), recovery (pumps restore gradients). A note adds that the K+ efflux during the downstroke is an active conductance change, not passive decay, and that nothing here is medical advice.

accessibility.alt: A voltage against time trace for one action potential, drawn left to right. It starts flat at rest near -70 mV, rises to a dashed threshold line near -55 mV, climbs steeply to a peak near +30 mV labelled Na+ influx, falls steeply through rest to a trough below -70 mV labelled K+ efflux, then returns to rest. A red dashed horizontal probe line with a dot on the voltage axis can be moved from -88 to +35 mV, so the learner can park it at rest, at threshold, at the peak or in the trough.
accessibility.reducedMotion: Show the finished trace in one frame with the five phases numbered left to right and each phase's ion written on it, plus a small table of resting, threshold and peak values (-70, -55, +30 mV), so the whole causal order is readable without motion.
